title: Pentatonic and blues
description: Major/minor pentatonic as subsets, relatives, and the blues b5 as color.

cards.front: What is a pentatonic scale?
cards.back: A five-note-per-octave scale. The two common ones are subsets of seven-note scales you already know.

cards.front: Give the major pentatonic formula and which degrees it omits.
cards.back: 1 2 3 5 6. Major scale without 4 and 7.

cards.front: Give the minor pentatonic formula and two ways to derive it.
cards.back: 1 b3 4 5 b7. Relative of major pentatonic (tonic on old degree 6). Also natural minor without 2 and b6.

cards.front: What is the blues-scale formula, and what is the extra note?
cards.back: 1 b3 4 b5 5 b7. The b5 is a chromatic passing note between 4 and 5 — color, not a core scale tone. Do not park on it.

cards.front: Why are pentatonic scales so stable?
cards.back: The omitted degrees are the ones that form half steps with their neighbours. Remove them and no two adjacent scale notes are a half step; gaps are whole steps or minor thirds.

cards.front: In major, which half-step pairs disappear when you drop 4 and 7?
cards.back: 4 sits a half step above 3; 7 sits a half step below 1.

cards.front: In natural minor, which degrees do you remove to get minor pentatonic, and why?
cards.back: Remove 2 and b6. Those sit in the half steps 2–b3 and 5–b6.

cards.front: Name the relative pair for A minor pentatonic and for A major pentatonic.
cards.back: A C D E G = C major pentatonic (C D E G A). A B C# E F# = F# minor pentatonic. Minor root is a minor third below its relative major.

cards.front: Does “works over many chords” mean it works over every chord?
cards.back: No. Each note has a relationship to the chord under it. That relationship is what you hear.

cards.front: Number A C D E G against Am, F, C, G, and E7. Which need care?
cards.back: Am: 1 b3 4 5 b7, all fit. F: 3 5 6 7 9, stress A and C. C: 6 1 9 3 5, fits. G: C is a half step above B — do not hold it. E7: G sits a half step below G#.

cards.front: Why does b3 over a dominant 7 work in blues?
cards.back: The idiom sets it up as deliberate tension against the chord’s major third, often by bending b3 up toward 3. A7 D7 E7 with minor pentatonic is the standard 12-bar sound.

cards.front: Outside the blues idiom, which pentatonic do you use over a major vs a minor chord?
cards.back: Major chord: major pentatonic of the chord’s root. Minor chord: minor pentatonic of its root. Hold only notes that are safe; a short passing note can touch almost anything.

cards.front: Give the familiar A minor pentatonic two-notes-per-string box, frets 5–8.
Where is the A blues note (Eb) in that 5–8 region?
cards.back: Between D and E: string 5 fret 6, and string 3 fret 8. Play D to Eb to E.

cards.front: A major pentatonic on string 6, and where is its root vs A minor pentatonic?
cards.back: E0 F#2 A5 B7 C#9 E12. Root A is still string 6 fret 5 — same place, different neighbors.

cards.front: Derive minor pentatonic for E, D, and G.
cards.back: E G A B D. D F G A C. G Bb C D F.

cards.front: Derive major pentatonic for G, D, and F.
cards.back: G A B D E. D E F# A B. F G A C D.

cards.front: What is the relative minor pentatonic of G major pentatonic?
cards.back: E minor pentatonic: E G A B D.

cards.front: Add the blues note to E minor pentatonic.
cards.back: E G A Bb B D. The b5 is Bb.

cards.front: E minor pentatonic on string 6, then the same classes on string 5 from fret 2.
cards.back: String 6 frets 0 3 5 7 10 12 = E G A B D E. String 5 frets 2 5 7 10 12 = B D E G A.
